title: Konjac or Shirataki: What It Is and Why It Has So Few Calories

seo.title: Shirataki Noodles: Why Konjac Is So Low in Calories
seo.meta_description: Shirataki noodles are mostly water held in a gel of konjac glucomannan, a highly water-binding soluble fiber. That is why a large serving can contain very little energy. Texture is springy and the noodles provide few nutrients beyond fiber.
seo.search_intent: Understand what konjac and shirataki are, why the noodles contain so few calories, how they differ from pasta, and which digestive cautions matter.

excerpt: Shirataki noodles are extremely low in calories because they are mostly water trapped in a gel made from glucomannan, the soluble fiber of Amorphophallus konjac. Glucomannan holds very large amounts of water and forms a stable structure with little dry matter. That creates noodle volume without the starch load of wheat pasta.
content_html:
Shirataki noodles are made mainly from water and konjac glucomannan, a soluble fiber extracted from the tuber of Amorphophallus konjac. Glucomannan's exceptional water-holding capacity creates a large serving with very little dry material.

This is why an entire package can provide far fewer calories than the same weight of cooked wheat pasta.

Glucomannan forms a highly hydrated gel

Glucomannan is a polysaccharide built mainly from glucose and mannose. Its long chains interact strongly with water and form very viscous solutions.

Shirataki production combines konjac flour with water and an alkaline setting agent to form a stable gel structure.

The finished noodle can be well over 90% water.

Low calories come from replacing starch with water and fiber

Traditional dry pasta contains a large amount of starch, which supplies metabolizable carbohydrate. Shirataki contains very little digestible dry matter.

Glucomannan is not digested like starch in the small intestine and much of it reaches the colon, where microbes can ferment it.

Nutrition labels therefore show very little energy per serving, although exact numbers depend on formulation.

Shirataki is not nutritionally equivalent to pasta

Few calories also means little protein, fat, and many micronutrients unless the product is fortified or blended.

Wheat and legume pastas provide substantial carbohydrate and protein, while pulse pasta can contribute considerable fiber too.

If shirataki replaces the entire starch base of a meal, build nutrition through the sauce, protein source, vegetables, and fats.

The texture is fundamentally different

Konjac gel is springy, resilient, and somewhat rubbery. It does not have a gluten network or the soft starch structure of conventional noodles.

Rinsing removes the characteristic packaging liquid odor. Dry-pan heating for a few minutes can remove surface water and help sauce cling.

Even then, shirataki does not absorb sauce exactly like wheat pasta.

Glucomannan can cause GI symptoms

It is a very viscous, fermentable fiber. Larger intakes can cause gas, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation in some people.

EFSA's review of konjac as a food additive did not require a numerical ADI at assessed uses, while gram-level doses in adults produced GI discomfort in some participants.

Individual tolerance and serving size matter.

Noodles are not the same as dry glucomannan supplements

Shirataki already contains fully hydrated fiber. Dry glucomannan supplements can expand greatly when exposed to water and need to be used exactly as directed.

There have also been historical choking problems with certain small konjac jelly candies whose shape and texture were unsuitable.

Those products are physically different from a plate of hydrated noodles.

Does konjac cause weight loss?

Replacing calorie-dense pasta with a very-low-energy base can reduce the energy of a meal if the rest of the meal does not compensate.

Trials of glucomannan supplements have produced mixed weight-loss findings, so the noodle should not be treated as a weight-loss drug.

Because the noodles contribute so little energy, a large bowl can look substantial while providing very little protein or fuel. That can be useful in some meals, but it also means the sauce and toppings need to do more nutritional work.

Products sometimes blend konjac with tofu, oat fiber, seaweed, or starch to alter texture. Those versions can contain more calories or protein than classic shirataki, so the label matters if the very-low-calorie feature is the reason you are buying them.

The practical rule: shirataki is low calorie because it is mostly water structured by konjac fiber. It is useful for volume, but it is not nutritionally interchangeable with protein- and starch-containing pasta.

faq.question: Why are shirataki noodles so low calorie?
faq.answer: They are mostly water plus a small amount of glucomannan fiber rather than a large amount of starch.

faq.question: Is konjac a fiber?
faq.answer: Yes. Its main functional component is glucomannan, a highly viscous soluble dietary fiber.

faq.question: Are shirataki the same as pasta?
faq.answer: No. They have much less energy and protein and a distinctly springy gel texture.
